2.text: with new ones, for our people consider a repaired sledge not fit for use in death. If something

3.text: broken and repaired breaks again on the trail of the dead, what would he (the dead one) do?

11.text: or received as a gift, are put aside. Things very bad, but one’s own, are put into use. I must say

12.text: the truth, the dead people are very bad people. They would not say, ‘Leave him alone!’¹

13.text: “Meanwhile, whence do the living people know all about it? To be sure, many of our people

14.text: come back from the trail of the dead. Probably they have made known the customs of the country
14.note: Machine draft added a trailing comma after ‘country’; zoomed at 100% and the line ends bare.

15.text: of the dead. Many dead ones are turned back by the power of incantations. Even I, when I was

16.text: rich, received several such incantations from hungry old women, gratifying their stomach with food.

17.text: But I am sorry to say that at present I have lost those incantations, being so poor.

18.text: “A man going along the trail of the dead may be turned back by a dog. The shaman bites

19.text: the left ear of the dog, and says to it, ‘Go and bring back thy master. We will feed thee with the

20.text: best food.’ (He may also be brought back with an incantation.) One with a slight disease may be

21.text: turned back where the trail is barred by a dog, which, springing at his face, makes him come back.

22.text: One with a serious disease would not yield. When a man coming back from the dead has turned
22.note: Machine draft added a trailing comma after ‘turned’; zoomed at 100% and the line ends bare (wraps into ‘back,’ on the next line).

23.text: back, the dog is killed. The Reindeer people keep dogs because they are very strong in bringing

24.text: back those dying ones. Is there any other use for them? We have to feed them. I cannot deny,

25.text: however, that the dog is good for many other uses. In hunting big game, he has a loud voice,

26.text: that is a useful protection against a bear met unexpectedly in the dark. You know it yourself. —

27.text: everybody has a dog, many of the people have dogs. When we travelled with you, nobody was

28.text: without a dog. In connection with this, when a man goes along the trail of the dead, it is useless

29.text: to take a reindeer for an incantation. The reindeer is full of fear. It runs from afar and exerts

30.text: no influence; it is only visible to eyes. To be sure, it appears (on the trail), but only from afar.

31.text: “And when a man is quite dead and has ceased breathing, those who are living do not weep

32.text: for him, — those looking (upon the world) members of his family. They do not weep shortly after

33.text: he is dead. Weeping is sinful. The one who has a slight disease is rejected by the dead. They

34.text: say, ‘Why did you come? Go away, go home.’ Then he goes away, returns home. It appears in

35.text: various ways. One may breathe, but he will lose his wits. In this case he probably has an hallu-

37.text: “Some people eat fly-agaric. Those from the Anadyr bring fly-agaric. Before eating, they say

38.text: to it, ‘Take me to the dead;’ and, indeed, they are taken there. He sinks down, falls into a swoon,

39.text: and then he is taken away, — not his body, but only his soul. And some one who has a hidden

40.text: disease may stay there forever. Therefore what has been said about the taking-away of clothes

41.text: must have become known through those who eat fly-agaric. Indeed, from three sources it may

42.text: become known, — from those who are turned back by dogs, from those sent back by the Merciful

43.text: Being because the dead have rejected them (these first two bring tidings), and from those who eat

45.text: “Little-Spoon, however, unexpectedly stopped his preparations, although before it seemed that

46.text: he had made up his mind. We had made all the necessary preparations, and were gathering our

47.text: sledges and the other things required; but we were disappointed, for evening came, and we were

48.text: still waiting in vain. Finally we could not wait any longer, and stopped our preparations. Evening

49.text: came, night came. We were speechless. He had only gorged himself. He had eaten the best and

50.text: sweetest morsels. I questioned his sons, and said to them, ‘Well, what is he doing?’ They replied,

51.text: ‘We will begin after he has eaten.’ Then they said, ‘He has gone to sleep.’ The sledge remained

52.text: behind the tent all night, as though in readiness for one really dead. The following morning, when

53.text: he awoke, he would not come out of the sleeping-room. He remained there all the time. Among
